features.title: QWC Core Network
features.body: Send and receive QWC on an open network. Independent nodes verify transactions and maintain the blockchain.

features.title: Privacy built in
features.body: QWC uses privacy technology to protect transaction details. Its open source code lets anyone examine how the network works.

features.title: RandomX proof of work
features.body: RandomX miners produce new blocks and secure the blockchain. Anyone can participate with compatible mining software.

features.title: Rewards for proven service
features.body: Service Nodes provide network services. Valid attestations establish eligibility, and the EPoSe protocol determines the reward rotation.

features.title: Service Nodes
features.body: Service Nodes support the network and take part in EPoSe. No QWC staking is required; block production remains the job of RandomX miners.

features.title: Web Wallet and open source
features.body: Use QWC directly in your browser with the Web Wallet. Explore the core software and contribute to its development on GitHub.

epose.title: Prove service. Earn QWC.
epose.body: EPoSe rewards registered Service Nodes for proven network services. The protocol evaluates valid attestations recorded on the blockchain and determines which nodes qualify for reward rotation.
epose.intro: QWC divides service time into EPoSe epochs. Service activity produces attestations, qualification is finalized, and only then can deterministic reward rotation use the qualified set.

compactCards.title: Provide service.
compactCards.body: Registered Service Nodes provide network services during each epoch.

compactCards.title: Verify service.
compactCards.body: Protocol-selected verifiers check service responses and submit signed attestations.

compactCards.title: Receive rewards.
compactCards.body: After qualification is finalized, eligible Service Nodes enter the protocol's deterministic reward rotation.

epose.originBody: Xecute developed the original EPoSe vision and contributed the Qwertycoin service-layer whitepaper. That work laid the foundation for rewarding useful network services.

steps.title: Register
steps.body: A Service Node publishes a signed registration with service identity, reward target, endpoint commitment, and admission proof.

steps.title: Serve
steps.body: The node provides QWC network service while normal RandomX mining remains responsible for block production.

steps.title: Attest
steps.body: Assigned verifiers challenge the Service Node and sign attestations only when the expected service response is valid.

steps.title: Qualify
steps.body: Chain state checks whether a registered node collected enough valid attestations for the relevant epoch.

steps.title: Reward
steps.body: Qualified nodes enter deterministic reward rotation. One selected payee can receive the EPoSe part of a block reward.

glossary.definition: A normal QWC node plus a registered service identity, endpoint commitment, reward address, and EPoSe participation data.
A fixed block period in which service activity is measured. Current parameter: {blocks} blocks, roughly {hours} hours at a {seconds} second block target.
The Service Node joined EPoSe by publishing a valid on-chain registration. Registered does not mean reward-eligible.
A signed confirmation from an assigned verifier that the Service Node answered its service challenge with the expected response.
A deterministic set of verifier nodes selected from chain state for a service challenge. The current public core targets {committee} verifiers when enough candidates exist.
A small proof attached to registration that makes identities cost work to create and helps reduce cheap Sybil registrations.
A registered Service Node that collected enough valid, non-duplicate attestations in the relevant epoch. The quorum is two thirds of the actually selected verifier committee.
The finalized epoch whose qualified set is used for the current reward period. In the current core, blocks in epoch N use qualified nodes from epoch N-1.
Qualified nodes are deterministically rotated as possible recipients of the EPoSe part of block rewards. The coinbase does not grow with the total node count.

epose.epochTitle: Epochs are block ranges, not clock appointments.
epose.epochBody: An EPoSe epoch is a {blocks}-block service period, roughly {hours} hours at the current {seconds}-second block target.

registeredVsQualified.label: Qualified
registeredVsQualified.body: The node proved enough service activity to become eligible for service rewards.

epose.committeeTitle: Verifier committees are not validator sets.
epose.committeeBody: Verifier committees do not produce blocks and do not replace RandomX miners. Their role is limited to checking Service Node activity for EPoSe qualification. The current public core targets {committee} verifiers when enough candidates exist and requires a two-thirds quorum of the actual committee. With a full committee, that means {fullCommitteeAttestations} attestations.
epose.rewardTimelineTitle: Service is measured first. Rewards follow later.

epose.rotationTitle: Reward rotation keeps block rewards compact.
epose.rotationBody: Current mainnet reward split: 90% miner / {rewardPercent}% EPoSe service reward. EPoSe service payouts are consensus-visible so every node can verify the selected Service Node and reward amount. Normal QWC wallet transactions continue to use the privacy mechanisms of the underlying QWC transaction model.
epose.rewardRulesBody: Every full node can verify reward eligibility and recipient selection from the blockchain. Subsidy allocation: 90% mining / {rewardPercent}% EPoSe service rewards; transaction fees remain with the miner.

faq.title: Wallets, the network and service nodes.

items.question: What is Qwertycoin?
items.answer: Qwertycoin (QWC) is a privacy-focused cryptocurrency with RandomX proof-of-work mining and EPoSe rewards for proven network services.

items.question: How do I use the Web Wallet?
items.answer: Open the official Web Wallet to create or restore a wallet for the current network and follow its safety instructions. Restoring a current-network wallet is not a way to import balances from the legacy blockchain. The main website never processes wallet keys.

items.question: Does EPoSe replace mining?
items.answer: No. RandomX miners produce blocks and secure the blockchain. EPoSe adds rewards for proven network services.

items.question: What is an epoch?
items.answer: An epoch is the block period used to assess EPoSe service activity. It currently spans {blocks} blocks, approximately {hours} hours at the target block interval.

items.question: What does qualified mean?
items.answer: A qualified Service Node has met the protocol's requirements for valid attestations in the relevant epoch and is eligible for service-reward selection. The technical quorum is at least ceil(2 x actual committee size / 3).

items.question: Who determines qualification and rewards?
items.answer: The EPoSe protocol. Every full node applies the same rules to valid on-chain registrations and attestations to verify eligibility and reward selection.

items.question: Do Service Nodes need to stake QWC?
items.answer: No. Participation requires EPoSe registration and the required service proofs, not locked QWC as stake.

items.question: Can one operator run multiple Service Nodes?
items.answer: Yes. Each Service Node needs its own valid registration and must meet the protocol's service requirements. Admission proof makes cheap identity creation harder.

items.question: Why is EPoSe not Proof of Stake?
items.answer: EPoSe rewards proven service rather than locked stake. Service Nodes verify blockchain data like other full nodes, while RandomX miners perform proof-of-work block production.

balances.question: Can I transfer my old Qwertycoin balance to the current network?
balances.answer: No. Balances from the legacy Qwertycoin blockchain cannot be imported, transferred or credited to the current network. Qwertycoin launched a separate blockchain with a fresh genesis in 2026. Updating a wallet, synchronizing it or entering an old seed does not move coins between these networks.

wallets.question: Can I use a wallet from before the 2026 relaunch?
wallets.answer: Wallets built for the legacy blockchain are not compatible with the current network. Download a supported wallet through the official Qwertycoin website and create a wallet for the current network. This does not recover or transfer an old balance. Keep existing wallet backups and private keys secure.

relaunch.question: Why did Qwertycoin launch a new blockchain?
relaunch.answer: Transition plans were already being discussed in 2023. The transition was inspired by the community and agreed jointly by community members and developers. It included a 1,000:1 swap, a different mining algorithm and a rebuild to address the problems of the legacy codebase dating back to 2018. Support for maintaining the old network had also declined, leaving its infrastructure dependent on too few operators. The separate 2026 blockchain uses RandomX Proof of Work and implements the long-awaited EPoSe service-node qualification and reward mechanism on a renewed codebase.

1000-to-1.question: Does the 1,000:1 ratio mean I can exchange my old coins now?
1000-to-1.answer: No. The 1,000:1 ratio refers to the community's historical swap proposal. It is not an exchange service available for balances remaining on the legacy blockchain. An old wallet balance does not create a claim to that balance divided by 1,000 on the current network.

backups.question: What should I do if I still have an old wallet?
backups.answer:
Keep the wallet file, seed and private keys secure. Never disclose your seed or private keys to anyone offering to migrate or recover the balance. If you also have a full backup of the legacy blockchain, contact the project through its official channels. A blockchain backup is different from a wallet backup; do not send wallet files or secret keys.

The current project cannot import that legacy balance into the new blockchain. To participate in the current network, use a supported wallet from the official Qwertycoin website. Check official project announcements regularly, as significant network changes can require action from holders.

keys.question: Have old wallets and private keys become invalid?
keys.answer: Not simply because the network was relaunched. Old wallet files and private keys have not been universally invalidated. Keys alone do not contain the blockchain history needed to locate and verify a balance. The current team no longer holds a copy of the legacy blockchain, no longer operates that infrastructure and is not aware of a surviving active full node. This does not prove that no private backup exists. Legacy wallets are not supported on the 2026 network, and their old balances cannot be imported into it.

chain-recovery.question: Could someone restore the old blockchain from a backup?
chain-recovery.answer: A complete, intact copy of the legacy blockchain could allow its history to be restored using compatible software and shared with other nodes. One surviving full copy can be enough to preserve that history. Processing new transactions would also require miners and a functioning network. A wallet file or seed alone cannot reconstruct the entire blockchain. Restoring the old chain would only restore the legacy network; it would never transfer its coins or balances into the 2026 network. Recovery cannot be guaranteed without examining the available blockchain data and software.

transition-token.question: Why was a temporary transition token created in 2025?
transition-token.answer:
Following discussions that began in 2023, the community-inspired transition was agreed jointly with the developers. The temporary transport token created in 2025 was intended to represent participating holders' balances during the transition and make a possible future allocation easier to account for if a successor network was launched. Its purpose was to preserve a route for participants from the original Qwertycoin project launched in 2018 to become involved again.

This historical purpose is not a promise of a current or future payout, and token balances are not automatically redeemable on the current network. Possible participation for transition-token holders remains in the planning stage; any confirmed arrangements will be announced through official channels. Legacy-chain balances and transition-token holdings are separate matters. Neither a restored old wallet nor the historical 1,000:1 ratio creates an automatic balance on the 2026 chain.

links.label: Historical 2025 announcement — not a current swap offer

network-support.question: Why did the old network stop operating, and how does EPoSe help?
network-support.answer:
A blockchain needs people to run nodes, store and distribute its history, maintain software and mine blocks. These activities require time, equipment, electricity and, for hosted infrastructure, ongoing server costs. Buying QWC from another holder on an exchange pays the seller; it does not automatically fund development or infrastructure. An offline wallet protects keys but does not keep the network running.

According to the project team, independent support for the old network gradually disappeared. By its final operating period in 2025, only two active servers were known to remain; these were eventually shut down because of the lack of users and activity. Voluntary operators cannot be expected to cover costs indefinitely.

The 2026 network combines RandomX Proof of Work with EPoSe, which rewards qualifying service-node operators for contributing infrastructure. This encourages independent participation but does not eliminate operating costs, guarantee profitability or replace miners and an active community.

no-premine.question: Did developers receive old balances or a special allocation in the relaunch?
no-premine.answer: No. The 2026 network launched without a premine or a reserved developer allocation. Developers' legacy balances were not automatically carried over either. The same protocol rules apply to developers and other participants: coins must be acquired or earned under the current network's rules, including mining or qualifying service-node rewards. This does not mean that everyone suffered the same losses, has the same resources or achieves the same mining results. The new technical foundation does not erase losses from the old network.

cards.title: Desktop wallets
cards.body: Download the current Qwertycoin GUI from the official GitHub release. GUI v2.0.2 users must install v2.0.5 once with the direct download because the v2.0.2 updater cannot follow GitHub's release-asset redirect. The Windows Setup and macOS DMG are the preferred installers; portable ZIP and TAR.GZ packages remain available as alternatives. Verify the download and checksum before use.
cards.note: Integrity note: SHA256SUMS verifies downloaded bytes, not publisher identity. Linux and Windows are unsigned; macOS is ad-hoc signed and not notarized.

cards.title: Docker image
cards.body: Run the verified Core release as a non-root Linux/amd64 container. Mainnet and the daemon are the defaults; the persistent named volume keeps chain data across container updates.
cards.note: The latest tag tracks the newest stable image. Audited production deployments may pin its image digest. Only P2P port 8196 is published below; administrative RPC is not exposed. Wallet and EPoSe identity data need separate protected volumes and the full quickstart.

commands.label: Start a persistent mainnet node
commands.code:
docker run -d --name qwertycoind --restart unless-stopped \
  -v qwertycoin-chain:/data -p 8196:8196 \
  docker.io/qwertycoin/qwertycoin:latest
